senses.d: Moving from place to place without a settled habitation; wandering.
Floating about without any certain direction; driven to and fro.
q: To heaven their prayers Flew up, nor missed the way, by envious winds Blown vagabond or frustrate.

senses.d: Being a vagabond; strolling and idle or vicious.

Vagabond.etym: [F., fr. L. vagabundus, from vagari to stroll about, from vagus strolling. See Vague.]

senses.d: One who wanders from place to place, having no fixed dwelling, or not abiding in it, and usually without the means of honest livelihood; a vagrant; a tramp; hence, a worthless person; a rascal.
q: A fugitive and a vagabond shalt thou be.

senses.d: To play the vagabond; to wander like a vagabond; to stroll.
q: On every part my vagabonding sight Did cast, and drown mine eyes in sweet delight.

senses.d: Same as Veil.
Avails; profit; return; proceeds.
q: My house is as 'twere the cave where the young outlaw hoards the stolen vails of his occupation.

senses.d: An unexpected gain or acquisition; a casual advantage or benefit; a windfall.
Money given to servants by visitors; a gratuity; — usually in the plural.
To let fall; to allow or cause to sink.
q: Vail your regard Upon a wronged, I would fain have said, a maid!

senses.d: To lower, or take off, in token of inferiority, reverence, submission, or the like.
q: France must vail her lofty-plumed crest!
Without vailing his bonnet or testifying any reverence for the alleged sanctity of the relic.

Vail.etym: [Aphetic form of avale. See Avale, Vale.]

senses.d: To yield or recede; to give place; to show respect by yielding, uncovering, or the like.
q: Thy convenience must vail to thy neighbor's necessity.

senses.d: Submission; decline; descent.
Having no real substance, value, or importance; empty; void; worthless; unsatisfying.
q: Every man walketh in a vain show.
Let no man deceive you with vain words.
Vain pomp, and glory of this world, I hate ye!
Vain wisdom all, and false philosophy.

senses.d: Destitute of force or efficacy; effecting no purpose; fruitless; ineffectual; as, vain toil; a vain attempt.
q: Bring no more vain oblations.
Vain is the force of man To crush the pillars which the pile sustain.

senses.d: Proud of petty things, or of trifling attainments; having a high opinion of one's own accomplishments with slight reason; conceited; puffed up; inflated.
q: But wilt thou know, O vain man, that faith apart from works is barren?
The minstrels played on every side, Vain of their art.

senses.d: Showy; ostentatious.
q: Load some vain church with old theatric state.

Vain.syn: Empty; worthless; fruitless; ineffectual; idle; unreal; shadowy; showy; ostentatious; light; inconstant; deceitful; delusive; unimportant; trifling.
Vain.etym: [F. vain, L. vanus empty, void, vain. Cf. Vanish, Vanity, Vaunt to boast.]

senses.d: Vanity; emptiness; — now used only in the phrase in vain.
Excessive vanity excited by one's own performances; empty pride; undue elation of mind; vain show; boastfulness.
q: He had nothing of vainglory.
The man's undone forever; for if Hector break not his neck i' the combat, he'll break't himself in vainglory.

senses.d: In a vain manner; in vain.
A tract of low ground, or of land between hills; a valley.
q: Beyond this vale of tears there is a life above.
In those fair vales, by nature formed to please.

Vale.etym: [OE. val, F. val, L. vallis; perhaps akin to Gr. ἔλοσ low ground, marsh meadow. Cf. Avalanche, Vail to lower, Valley.]

senses.d: Vigorous in body; strong; powerful; as, a valiant fencer.
Intrepid in danger; courageous; brave.
q: A valiant and most expert gentleman.
And Saul said to David . . . be thou valiant for me, and fight the Lord's battles.

senses.d: Performed with valor or bravery; heroic.
q: have made such valiant confessions.

Valiant.etym: [OE. valiant, F. vaillant, OF. vaillant, valant, originally p. pr. of OF. & F. valoir to be worth, L. valere to be strong. See Wield, and cf. Avail, Convalesce, Equivalent, Prevail, Valid.]

senses.d: The space inclosed between ranges of hills or mountains; the strip of land at the bottom of the depressions intersecting a country, including usually the bed of a stream, with frequently broad alluvial plains on one or both sides of the stream. Also used figuratively.
q: The valley of the shadow of death.
Sweet interchange Of hill and valley, rivers, woods, and plains.

senses.d: The place of meeting of two slopes of a roof, which have their plates running in different directions, and form on the plan a reëntrant angle.

Valley.etym: [OE. vale, valeie, OF. valée, valede, F. vallée, LL. vallata, L. vallis, valles. See Vale.]

senses.d: The property or aggregate properties of a thing by which it is rendered useful or desirable, or the degree of such property or sum of properties; worth; excellence; utility; importance.
q: Ye are all physicians of no value.
Ye are of more value than many sparrows.
Cæsar is well acquainted with your virtue, And therefore sets this value on your life.
Before events shall have decided on the value of the measures.

senses.d: Worth estimated by any standard of purchasing power, especially by the market price, or the amount of money agreed upon as an equivalent to the utility and cost of anything.
q: An article may be possessed of the highest degree of utility, or power to minister to our wants and enjoyments, and may be universally made use of, without possessing exchangeable value.
Value is the power to command commodities generally.
Value is the generic term which expresses power in exchange.
His design was not to pay him the value of his pictures, because they were above any price.

senses.d: Precise signification; import; as, the value of a word; the value of a legal instrument
Esteem; regard.
q: My relation to the person was so near, and my value for him so great

senses.d: The relative length or duration of a tone or note, answering to quantity in prosody; thus, a quarter note has the value of two eighth notes .
In an artistical composition, the character of any one part in its relation to other parts and to the whole; — often used in the plural; as, the values are well given, or well maintained.
Valor.

Value.etym: [OF. value, fr. valoir, p. p. valu, to be worth, fr. L. valere to be strong, to be worth. See Valiant.]

senses.d: To estimate the value, or worth, of; to rate at a certain price; to appraise; to reckon with respect to number, power, importance, etc.
q: The mind doth value every moment.
The queen is valued thirty thousand strong.
The king must take it ill, That he's so slightly valued in his messenger.
Neither of them valued their promises according to rules of honor or integrity.

senses.d: To rate highly; to have in high esteem; to hold in respect and estimation; to appreciate; to prize; as, to value one for his works or his virtues.
q: Which of the dukes he values most.

senses.d: To raise to estimation; to cause to have value, either real or apparent; to enhance in value.
q: Some value themselves to their country by jealousies of the crown.

senses.d: To be worth; to be equal to in value.
q: The peace between the French and us not values The cost that did conclude it.

Value.syn: To compute; rate; appraise; esteem; respect; regard; estimate; prize; appreciate.

senses.d: That property of a color by which it is distinguished as bright or dark; luminosity.
Any particular quantitative determination; as, a function's value for some special value of its argument.

The valuable ingredients to be obtained by treatment from any mass or compound; specif., the precious metals contained in rock, gravel, or the like; as, the vein carries good values; the values on the hanging walls.
Highly regarded; esteemed; prized; as, a valued contributor; a valued friend.
To pass from a visible to an invisible state; to go out of sight; to disappear; to fade; as, vapor vanishes from the sight by being dissipated; a ship vanishes from the sight of spectators on land.
q: The horse vanished . . . out of sight.
Go; vanish into air; away!
The champions vanished from their posts with the speed of lightning.
Gliding from the twilight past to vanish among realities.

senses.d: To be annihilated or lost; to pass away.

Vanish.etym: [OE. vanissen, OF. vanir (in comp.): cf. OF. envanir, esvanir, esvanuïr, F. s'évanouir; fr. L. vanus empty, vain; cf. L. vanescere, evanescere, to vanish. See Vain, and cf. Evanescent,-ish.]

senses.d: The brief terminal part of a vowel or vocal element, differing more or less in quality from the main part; as, a as in ale ordinarily ends with a vanish of i as in ill, o as in old with a vanish of oo as in foot.
The quality or state of being vain; want of substance to satisfy desire; emptiness; unsubstantialness; unrealness; falsity.
q: Vanity of vanities, saith the Preacher, vanity of vanities; all is vanity.
Here I may well show the vanity of that which is reported in the story of Walsingham.

senses.d: An inflation of mind upon slight grounds; empty pride inspired by an overweening conceit of one's personal attainments or decorations; an excessive desire for notice or approval; pride; ostentation; conceit.
q: The exquisitely sensitive vanity of Garrick was galled.

senses.d: That which is vain; anything empty, visionary, unreal, or unsubstantial; fruitless desire or effort; trifling labor productive of no good; empty pleasure; vain pursuit; idle show; unsubstantial enjoyment.
q: Vanity of vanities, saith the Preacher.
Vanity possesseth many who are desirous to know the certainty of things to come.
with vanity had filled the works of men.
Think not, when woman's transient breath is fled, That all her vanities at once are dead; Succeeding vanities she still regards.

senses.d: One of the established characters in the old moralities and puppet shows. See Morality, n., 5.
q: You . . . take vanity the puppet's part.

Vanity.syn: Egotism; pride; emptiness; worthlessness; self-sufficiency. See Egotism, and Pride.
Vanity.etym: [OE. vanite, F. vanité, L. vanitas, fr. vanus empty, vain. See Vain.]

senses.d: Having the capacity of varying or changing; capable of alternation in any manner; changeable; as, variable winds or seasons; a variable quantity.
Liable to vary; too susceptible of change; mutable; fickle; unsteady; inconstant; as, the affections of men are variable; passions are variable.
q: Lest that thy love prove likewise variable.
His heart, I know, how variable and vain!

Variable.syn: Changeable; mutable; fickle; wavering; unsteady; versatile; inconstant.

senses.d: That which is variable; that which varies, or is subject to change.

A quantity which may increase or decrease; a quantity which admits of an infinite number of values in the same expression; a variable quantity; as, in the equation x2 - y2 = R2, x and y are variables.
A shifting wind, or one that varies in force.
The quality or state of being variable; variability.
The quality or state of being variant; change of condition; variation.
Difference that produces dispute or controversy; disagreement; dissension; discord; dispute; quarrel.
q: That which is the strength of their amity shall prove the immediate author of their variance.

senses.d: A disagreement or difference between two parts of the same legal proceeding, which, to be effectual, ought to agree, — as between the writ and the declaration, or between the allegation and the proof.
To boast; to make a vain display of one's own worth, attainments, decorations, or the like; to talk ostentatiously; to brag.
q: Pride, which prompts a man to vaunt and overvalue what he is, does incline him to disvalue what he has.

Vaunt.etym: [F. vanter, LL. vanitare, fr. L. vanus vain. See Vain.]

senses.d: To boast of; to make a vain display of; to display with ostentation.
q: Charity vaunteth not itself, is not puffed up.
My vanquisher, spoiled of his vaunted spoil.

senses.d: A vain display of what one is, or has, or has done; ostentation from vanity; a boast; a brag.
q: The spirits beneath, whom I seduced With other promises and other vaunts.

senses.d: The first part.

Vaunt.etym: [F. avant before, fore. See Avant, Vanguard.]

senses.d: To put forward; to display.
q: And what so else his person most may vaunt.

senses.d: Acting with great force; furious; violent; impetuous; forcible; mighty; as, a vehement wind; a vehement torrent; a vehement fire or heat.
Very ardent; very eager or urgent; very fervent; passionate; as, a vehement affection or passion.

Vehement.syn: Furious; violent; raging; impetuous; passionate; ardent; eager; hot; fervid; burning.
Vehement.etym: [L. vehemens, the first part of which is perhaps akin to vehere to carry, and the second mens mind: cf. F. véhément. Cf. Vehicle, and Mental.]

senses.d: In a vehement manner.
Something hung up, or spread out, to intercept the view, and hide an object; a cover; a curtain; esp., a screen, usually of gauze, crape, or similar diaphnous material, to hide or protect the face.
q: The veil of the temple was rent in twain.
She, as a veil down to the slender waist, Her unadornéd golden tresses wore.

senses.d: A cover; a disguise; a mask; a pretense.
q: pluck the borrowed veil of modesty from the so seeming Mistress Page.

senses.d: The calyptra of mosses.
A covering for a person or thing; as, a nun's veil; a paten veil; an altar veil.
Same as Velum, 3.

Veil.etym: [OE. veile, OF. veile, F. voile, L. velum a sail, covering, curtain, veil, probably fr. vehere to bear, carry, and thus originally, that which bears the ship on. See Vehicle, and cf. Reveal.]

senses.d: To throw a veil over; to cover with a veil.
q: Her face was veiled; yet to my fancied sight, Love, sweetness, goodness, in her person shined.

senses.d: Fig.: To invest; to cover; to hide; to conceal.
q: To keep your great pretenses veiled.

Veil.etym: [Cf. OF. veler, F. voiler, L. velarc. See Veil, n.]

senses.d: One of the vessels which carry blood, either venous or arterial, to the heart. See Artery, 2.
One of the similar branches of the framework of a leaf.
One of the ribs or nervures of the wings of insects. See Venation.

A narrow mass of rock intersecting other rocks, and filling inclined or vertical fissures not corresponding with the stratification; a lode; a dike; — often limited, in the language of miners, to a mineral vein or lode, that is, to a vein which contains useful minerals or ores.
A fissure, cleft, or cavity, as in the earth or other substance.
q: Let the glass of the prisms be free from veins.

senses.d: A streak or wave of different color, appearing in wood, and in marble and other stones; variegation.
A train of associations, thoughts, emotions, or the like; a current; a course.
q: He can open a vein of true and noble thinking.

senses.d: Peculiar temper or temperament; tendency or turn of mind; a particular disposition or cast of genius; humor; strain; quality; also, manner of speech or action; as, a rich vein of humor; a satirical vein.
q: Certain discoursing wits which are of the same veins.
Invoke the Muses, and improve my vein.

senses.d: To form or mark with veins; to fill or cover with veins.
Punishment inflicted in return for an injury or an offense; retribution; — often, in a bad sense, passionate or unrestrained revenge.
q: To me belongeth vengeance and recompense.
To execute fierce vengeance on his foes.

senses.d: Harm; mischief.

Vengeance.etym: [F. vengeance, fr. venger to avenge, L. vindicare to lay claim to, defend, avenge, fr. vindex a claimant, defender, avenger, the first part of which is of uncertain origin, and the last part akin to dicere to say. See Diction, and cf. Avenge, Revenge, Vindicate.]

senses.d: Beasts of the chase.
Formerly, the flesh of any of the edible beasts of the chase, also of game birds; now, the flesh of animals of the deer kind exclusively.

Venison.etym: [OE. veneison, veneson, venison, OF. veneison, F. venaison, L. venatio hunting, the chase, game, fr. venari, p. p. venatus, to hunt; perhaps akin to OHG. weidinōn, weidenen, to pasture, to hunt, G. weide pasturage. Cf. Gain to acquire, Venation.]

senses.d: Matter fatal or injurious to life; poison; particularly, the poisonous matter which certain animals, such as serpents, scorpions, bees, etc., secrete in a state of health, and communicate by biting or stinging.
q: Or hurtful worm with cankered venom bites.

senses.d: Spite; malice; malignity; evil quality. Chaucer.

Venom.etym: [OE. venim, OF. venim, venin, F. venin, L. venenum. Cf. Venenate.]

senses.d: To infect with venom; to envenom; to poison.

Venom.etym: [OE. venimen, OF. venimer, L. venenare. See Venom, n.]

senses.d: Full of venom; noxious to animal life; poisonous; as, the bite of a serpent may be venomous.
Having a poison gland or glands for the secretion of venom, as certain serpents and insects.
Noxious; mischievous; malignant; spiteful; as, a venomous progeny; a venomous writer.

Venomous.etym: [OE. venemous, venimous, F. venimeux, L. venenosus, fr. venenum poison. See Venom, and cf. Venenose.]

senses.d: Sale; opportunity to sell; market.
q: There is no vent for any commodity but of wool.

Vent.etym: [F. vente, fr. L. vendere, -itum, to sell; perh. confused with E. vent an opening. See Vend.]

senses.d: To sell; to vend.
q: Therefore did those nations vent such spice.

senses.d: A baiting place; an inn.

Vent.etym: [Sp. venta a poor inn, sale, market. See Vent sale.]

senses.d: To snuff; to breathe or puff out; to snort.

Vent.etym: [Cf. F. venter to blow, vent wind (see Ventilate); but prob influenced by E. vent an opening.]

senses.d: A small aperture; a hole or passage for air or any fluid to escape; as, the vent of a cask; the vent of a mold; a volcanic vent.
q: Look, how thy wounds do bleed at many vents.
Long 't was doubtful, both so closely pent, Which first should issue from the narrow vent.

senses.d: The anal opening of certain invertebrates and fishes; also, the external cloacal opening of reptiles, birds, amphibians, and many fishes.
The opening at the breech of a firearm, through which fire is communicated to the powder of the charge; touchhole.
Sectional area of the passage for gases divided by the length of the same passage in feet.
Fig.: Opportunity of escape or passage from confinement or privacy; outlet.
Emission; escape; passage to notice or expression; publication; utterance.
q: Without the vent of words.
Thou didst make tolerable vent of thy travel.

Vent.etym: [OE. fent, fente, a slit, F. fente a slit, cleft, fissure, from fendre to split, L. findere; but probably confused with F. vent wind, L. ventus. See Fissure, and cf. Vent to snuff.]

senses.d: To let out at a vent, or small aperture; to give passage or outlet to.
To suffer to escape from confinement; to let out; to utter; to pour forth; as, to vent passion or complaint.
q: The queen of heaven did thus her fury vent.

senses.d: To utter; to report; to publish.
q: By mixing somewhat true to vent more lies.
Thou hast framed and vented very curious orations.

senses.d: To scent, as a hound.
To furnish with a vent; to make a vent in; as, to vent. a mold.
An undertaking of chance or danger; the risking of something upon an event which can not be foreseen with certainty; a hazard; a risk; a speculation.
q: I, in this venture, double gains pursue.

senses.d: An event that is not, or can not be, foreseen; an accident; chance; hap; contingency; luck.
The thing put to hazard; a stake; a risk; especially, something sent to sea in trade.
q: My ventures are not in one bottom trusted.
A certain man drew a bow at a venture.
A bargain at a venture made.

Venture.etym: [Aphetic form of OE. aventure. See Adventure.]

senses.d: To hazard one's self; to have the courage or presumption to do, undertake, or say something; to dare.
To make a venture; to run a hazard or risk; to take the chances.
q: Who freights a ship to venture on the seas.

senses.d: To expose to hazard; to risk; to hazard; as, to venture one's person in a balloon.
q: I am afraid; and yet I'll venture it.

senses.d: To put or send on a venture or chance; as, to venture a horse to the West Indies.
To confide in; to rely on; to trust.
q: A man would be well enough pleased to buy silks of one whom he would not venture to feel his pulse.

senses.d: To prove to be true or correct; to establish the truth of; to confirm; to substantiate.
q: This is verified by a number of examples.
So shalt thou best fulfill, best verify. The prophets old, who sung thy endless reign.

senses.d: To confirm or establish the authenticity of by examination or competent evidence; to authenciate; as, to verify a written statement; to verify an account, a pleading, or the like.
q: To verify our title with their lives.

senses.d: To maintain; to affirm; to support.

Verify.etym: [F. vérifier, LL. verificare, from L. verus true + -ficare to make. See Very, and -fy.]

senses.d: In very truth; beyond doubt or question; in fact; certainly.
q: Trust in the Lord and do good; so shalt thou dwell in the ��nd, and verily thou shalt be fed.

senses.d: The quality or state of being true, or real; consonance of a statement, proposition, or other thing, with fact; truth; reality.
q: It is a proposition of eternal verity, that none can govern while he is despised.

senses.d: That which is true; a true assertion or tenet; a truth; a reality.
q: Mark what I say, which you shall find By every syllable a faithful verity.

Verity.etym: [F. vérité, L. veritas, fr. verus true. See Very.]

senses.d: A bright red pigment consisting of mercuric sulphide, obtained either from the mineral cinnabar or artificially. It has a fine red color, and is much used in coloring sealing wax, in printing, etc.
Hence, a red color like the pigment; a lively and brilliant red; as, cheeks of vermilion.
To color with vermilion, or as if with vermilion; to dye red; to cover with a delicate red.
True; real; actual; veritable.
q: Whether thou be my very son Esau or not.
He that covereth a transgression seeketh love; but he that repeateth a matter separateth very friends.
The very essence of truth is plainness and brightness.
I looked on the consideration of public service or public ornament to be real and very justice.

Very.etym: [OE. verai, verray, OF. verai, vrai, F. vrai, (assumed) LL. veracus, for L. verax true, veracious, fr. verus true; akin to OHG. & OS. wār, G. wahr, D. waar; perhaps originally, that is or exists, and akin to E. was. Cf. Aver, v. t., Veracious, Verdict, Verity.]

senses.d: In a high degree; to no small extent; exceedingly; excessively; extremely; as, a very great mountain; a very bright sun; a very cold day; the river flows very rapidly; he was very much hurt.
A hollow or concave utensil for holding anything; a hollow receptacle of any kind, as a hogshead, a barrel, a firkin, a bottle, a kettle, a cup, a bowl, etc.
q: out of these noble vessels.

senses.d: A general name for any hollow structure made to float upon the water for purposes of navigation; especially, one that is larger than a common rowboat; as, a war vessel; a passenger vessel.
q: began to build a vessel of huge bulk.

senses.d: Fig.: A person regarded as receiving or containing something; esp. (Script.), one into whom something is conceived as poured, or in whom something is stored for use; as, vessels of wrath or mercy.
q: He is a chosen vessel unto me.
fit vessel, fittest imp of fraud, in whom To enter.

senses.d: Any tube or canal in which the blood or other fluids are contained, secreted, or circulated, as the arteries, veins, lymphatics, etc.

A continuous tube formed from superposed large cylindrical or prismatic cells (tracheæ), which have lost their intervening partitions, and are usually marked with dots, pits, rings, or spirals by internal deposition of secondary membranes; a duct.

Vessel.etym: [OF. vessel, veissel, vaissel, vaissiel, F. vaisseau, fr. L. vascellum, dim. of vasculum, dim. of vas a vessel. Cf. Vascular, Vase.]

senses.d: To put into a vessel.
A covering or garment; some part of clothing or dress
any priestly garment.
q: The sculptor could not give vestments suitable to the quality of the persons represented.

Vestment.etym: [OE. vestement, vestiment, OF. vestement, vestiment, F. vêtement, fr. L. vestimentum, fr. vestire to clothe, fr. vestis a garment, clothing. See Vest.]

senses.d: A room appendant to a church, in which sacerdotal vestments and sacred utensils are sometimes kept, and where meetings for worship or parish business are held; a sacristy; — formerly called revestiary.
q: He said unto him that was over the vestry, Bring forth vestments for all the worshipers of Baal.

senses.d: A parochial assembly; an assembly of persons who manage parochial affairs; — so called because usually held in a vestry.
A body, composed of wardens and vestrymen, chosen annually by a parish to manage its temporal concerns.

Vestry.etym: [OE. vestrye, F. vestiaire, L. vestiarium, fr. vestiarius belonging to clothes, fr. vestis a garment. See Vest, n., and cf. Vestiary.]

senses.d: A garment or garments; a robe; clothing; dress; apparel; vestment; covering; envelope.
q: Approach, and kiss her sacred vesture's hem.
Rocks, precipices, and gulfs, appareled with a vesture of plants.
There polished chests embroidered vestures graced.

senses.d: The corn, grass, underwood, stubble, etc., with which land was covered; as, the vesture of an acre.

Vesture.etym: [OF. vesture, vesteure, F. vêture, LL. vestitura, from L. vestire to clothe, dress. See Vest, v. t., and cf. Vestiture.]

senses.d: To toss back and forth; to agitate; to disquiet.
q: White curl the waves, and the vexed ocean roars.

senses.d: To make angry or annoyed by little provocations; to irritate; to plague; to torment; to harass; to afflict; to trouble; to tease.
q: Ten thousand torments vex my heart.

senses.d: To twist; to weave.
q: Some English wool, vexed in a Belgian loom.

Vex.etym: [F. vexer, L. vexare, vexatum, to vex, originally, to shake, toss, in carrying, v. intens. fr. vehere, vectum, to carry. See Vehicle.]

senses.d: To be irritated; to fret.
The act of vexing, or the state of being vexed; agitation; disquiet; trouble; irritation.
q: Passions too violent . . . afford us nothing but vexation and pain.
Those who saw him after a defeat looked in vain for any trace of vexation.

senses.d: The cause of trouble or disquiet; affliction.
q: Your children were vexation to your youth.

senses.d: A harassing by process of law; a vexing or troubling, as by a malicious suit.

Vexation.syn: Chagrin; agitation; mortification; uneasiness; trouble; grief; sorrow; distress. See Chagrin.

senses.d: Annoyed; harassed; troubled.
Much debated or contested; causing discussion; as, a vexed question.
A small bottle, usually of glass; a little glass vessel with a narrow aperture intended to be closed with a stopper; as, a vial of medicine.
q: Take thou this vial, being then in bed, And this distilled liquor drink thou off.

Vial.etym: [OE. viole, fiole, F. fiole. See Phial.]

senses.d: To put in a vial or vials.
The defeat of an enemy in battle, or of an antagonist in any contest; a gaining of the superiority in any struggle or competition; conquest; triumph; — the opposite of defeat.
q: Death is swallowed up in victory.
God on our side, doubt not of victory.
Victory may be honorable to the arms, but shameful to the counsels, of a nation.

Victory.etym: [OE. victorie, OF. victorie, victoire, F. victoire, L. victoria. See Victor.]

senses.d: Food; — now used chiefly in the plural. See Victuals.
q: He was not able to keep that place three days for lack of victual.
There came a fair-hair'd youth, that in his hand Bare victual for the mowers.
Short allowance of victual.

senses.d: Grain of any kind.
To supply with provisions for subsistence; to provide with food; to store with sustenance; as, to victual an army; to victual a ship.
q: I must go victual Orleans forthwith.

senses.d: Food for human beings, esp. when it is cooked or prepared for the table; that which supports human life; provisions; sustenance; meat; viands.
q: Then had we plenty of victuals.

Victuals.etym: [OE. vitaille, OF. vitaille, F. victuaille, pl. victuailles, fr. L. victualia, pl. of. victualis belonging to living or nourishment, fr. victus nourishment, from vivere, victum, to live; akin to vivus living. See Vivid.]

senses.d: The act of seeing or beholding; sight; look; survey; examination by the eye; inspection.
q: Thenceforth I thought thee worth my nearer view.
Objects near our view are thought greater than those of a larger size that are more remote.
Surveying nature with too nice a view.

senses.d: Mental survey; intellectual perception or examination; as, a just view of the arguments or facts in a case.
q: I have with exact view perused thee, Hector.

senses.d: Power of seeing, either physically or mentally; reach or range of sight; extent of prospect.
q: The walls of Pluto's palace are in view.

senses.d: That which is seen or beheld; sight presented to the natural or intellectual eye; scene; prospect; as, the view from a window.
q: 'T is distance lends enchantment to the view.

senses.d: The pictorial representation of a scene; a sketch, either drawn or painted; as, a fine view of Lake George.
Mode of looking at anything; manner of apprehension; conception; opinion; judgment; as, to state one's views of the policy which ought to be pursued.
q: To give a right view of this mistaken part of liberty.

senses.d: That which is looked towards, or kept in sight, as object, aim, intention, purpose, design; as, he did it with a view of escaping.
q: No man sets himself about anything but upon some view or other which serves him for a reason.

senses.d: Appearance; show; aspect.
q: which, by the splendor of her view Dazzled, before we never knew.

View.etym: [OF. veue, F. vue, fr. OF. veoir to see, p. p. veu, F. voir, p. p. vu, fr. L. videre to see. See Vision, and cf. Interview, Purview, Review, Vista.]

senses.d: To see; to behold; especially, to look at with attention, or for the purpose of examining; to examine with the eye; to inspect; to explore.
q: O, let me view his visage, being dead.
Nearer to view his prey, and, unespied, To mark what of their state he more might learn.

senses.d: To survey or examine mentally; to consider; as, to view the subject in all its aspects.
q: The happiest youth, viewing his progress through.

senses.d: Attentive to discover and avoid danger, or to provide for safety; wakeful; watchful; circumspect; wary.
q: Sirs, take your places, and be vigilant.

Vigilant.etym: [L. vigilans, -antis, p. pr. of vigilare to watch, fr. vigil awake: cf. F. vigilant. See Vigil.]

senses.d: Low; base; worthless; mean; despicable.
q: A poor man in vile raiment.
The craft either of fishing, which was Peter's, or of making tents, which was Paul's, were more vile than the science of physic.
The inhabitants account gold but as a vile thing.

senses.d: Morally base or impure; depraved by sin; hateful in the sight of God and men; sinful; wicked; bad.
q: Behold, I am vile; what shall I answer thee ?

Vile.etym: [OE. vil, F. vil, from L. vilis cheap, worthless, vile, base.]

senses.d: A small assemblage of houses in the country, less than a town or city.

Village.etym: [F., fr. L. villaticus belonging to a country house or villa. See Villa, and cf. Villatic.]

senses.d: Any woody climbing plant which bears grapes.

Hence, a climbing or trailing plant; the long, slender stem of any plant that trails on the ground, or climbs by winding round a fixed object, or by seizing anything with its tendrils, or claspers; a creeper; as, the hop vine; the bean vine; the vines of melons, squashes, pumpkins, and other cucurbitaceous plants.
q: There shall be no grapes on the vine.
And one went out into the field to gather herbs, and found a wild vine, and gathered thereof wild gourds.

Vine.etym: [F. vigne, L. vinea a vineyard, vine from vineus of or belonging to wine, vinum wine, grapes. See Wine, and cf. Vignette.]

senses.d: One who cultivates, prunes, or cares for, grapevines; a laborer in a vineyard.
q: The sons of the shall be your plowmen and your vinedressers.

senses.d: A sour liquid used as a condiment, or as a preservative, and obtained by the spontaneous (acetous) fermentation, or by the artificial oxidation, of wine, cider, beer, or the like.
Hence, anything sour; — used also metaphorically.
q: Here's the challenge: . . . I warrant there's vinegar and pepper in't.

Vinegar.etym: [OE. vinegre, F. vinaigre; vin wine (L. vinum) + aigre sour. See Wine, and Eager, a.]

senses.d: To convert into vinegar; to make like vinegar; to render sour or sharp.
q: Hoping that he hath vinegared his senses As he was bid.

senses.d: An inclosure or yard for grapevines; a plantation of vines producing grapes.

Vineyard.etym: [For OE. winyard, AS. wīngeard; influenced by E. vine. See Wine, and Yard an inclosure.]

senses.d: The produce of the vine for one season, in grapes or in wine; as, the vintage is abundant; the vintage of 1840.
The act or time of gathering the crop of grapes, or making the wine for a season.

Vintage.etym: [Corrupted by influence of vintner, vintry, from OE. vindage, vendage, for vendange, OF. vendenge, F. vendange, from L. vindemia; vinum wine, grapes + demere to take off; de + emere, originally, to take. See Wine, Redeem, and cf. Vindemial.]

senses.d: A stringed musical instrument formerly in use, of the same form as the violin, but larger, and having six strings, to be struck with a bow, and the neck furnished with frets for stopping the strings.
q: Me softer airs befit, and softer strings Of lute, or viol still, more apt for mournful things.

senses.d: A large rope sometimes used in weighing anchor.

Viol.etym: [F. viole; cf. Pr. viola, viula, Sp., Pg., & It. viola, LL. vitula; of uncertain origin; perhaps from L. vitulari to celebrate a festival, keep holiday, be joyful, perhaps originally, to sacrifice a calf (vitulus; cf. Veal). Cf. Fiddle, Vielle, 2d Viola, Violin.]

senses.d: To treat in a violent manner; to abuse.
q: His wife Boadicea violated with stripes, his daughters with rape.

senses.d: To do violence to, as to anything that should be held sacred or respected; to profane; to desecrate; to break forcibly; to trench upon; to infringe.
q: Violated vows 'Twixt the souls of friend and friend.
Oft have they violated The temple, oft the law, with foul affronts.

senses.d: To disturb; to interrupt.
To commit rape on; to ravish; to outrage.

Violate.syn: To injure; disturb; interrupt; infringe; transgress; profane; deflour; debauch; dishonor.
Violate.etym: [L. violatus, p. p. of violare to violate, fr. vis strength, force. See Violent.]

senses.d: The quality or state of being violent; highly excited action, whether physical or moral; vehemence; impetuosity; force.
q: That seal You ask with such a violence, the king, Mine and your master, with his own hand gave me.
All the elements At least had gone to wrack, disturbed and torn With the violence of this conflict.

senses.d: Injury done to that which is entitled to respect, reverence, or observance; profanation; infringement; unjust force; outrage; assault.
q: Do violence to do man.
We can not, without offering violence to all records, divine and human, deny an universal deluge.
Looking down, he saw The whole earth filled with violence.

senses.d: Ravishment; rape; constupration.

Violence.syn: Vehemence; outrage; fierceness; eagerness; violation; infraction; infringement; transgression; oppression.

senses.d: To assault; to injure; also, to bring by violence; to compel.

Moving or acting with physical strength; urged or impelled with force; excited by strong feeling or passion; forcible; vehement; impetuous; fierce; furious; severe; as, a violent blow; the violent attack of a disease.
q: Float upon a wild and violent sea.
A violent cross wind from either coast.

senses.d: Acting, characterized, or produced by unjust or improper force; outrageous; unauthorized; as, a violent attack on the right of free speech.
q: To bring forth more violent deeds.
Some violent hands were laid on Humphrey's life.

senses.d: Produced or effected by force; not spontaneous; unnatural; abnormal.
q: These violent delights have violent ends.
No violent state can be perpetual.
Ease would recant Vows made in pain, as violent and void.

Violent.syn: Fierce; vehement; outrageous; boisterous; turbulent; impetuous; passionate; severe; extreme.
Violent.etym: [F., from L. violentus, from vis strength, force; probably akin to Gr. � a muscle, strength.]

senses.d: An assailant.
To urge with violence.
To be violent; to act violently.
q: The grief is fine, full, perfect, that I taste, An violenteth in a sense as strong As that which causeth it.

senses.d: In a violent manner.
Any one of numerous species of Old World venomous makes belonging to Vipera, Clotho, Daboia, and other genera of the family Viperidæ.
q: There came a viper out of the heat, and fastened on his hand.

senses.d: A dangerous, treacherous, or malignant person.
q: Who committed To such a viper his most sacred trust Of secrecy.

Viper.etym: [F. vipère, L. vipera, probably contr. fr. vivipera; vivus alive + parere to bring forth, because it was believed to be the only serpent that brings forth living young. Cf. Quick, a., Parent, Viviparous, Wivern, Weever.]

senses.d: A woman who has had no carnal knowledge of man; a maid.
A person of the male sex who has not known sexual indulgence.
q: These are they which were not defiled with women; for they are virgins.
He his flesh hath overcome; He was a virgin, as he said.

senses.d: Any one of several species of gossamer-winged butterflies of the family Lycænidæ.
A female insect producing eggs from which young are hatched, though there has been no fecundation by a male; a parthenogenetic insect.

Virgin.etym: [L. virgo, -inis: cf. OF. virgine, virgene, virge, vierge, F. vierge.]

senses.d: Being a virgin; chaste; of or pertaining to a virgin; becoming a virgin; maidenly; modest; indicating modesty; as, a virgin blush.
q: Innocence and virgin modesty . . . That would be wooed, and unsought be won.

senses.d: Pure; undefiled; unmixed; fresh; new; as, virgin soil; virgin gold.
q: The white cold virgin snow upon my heart.
A few ounces of mutton, with a little virgin oil.

senses.d: Not yet pregnant; impregnant.
To act the virgin; to be or keep chaste; — followed by it. See It, 5.
The quality or state of being a virgin; undefiled purity or chastity; maidenhood.
The unmarried life; celibacy.
Manly strength or courage; bravery; daring; spirit; valor.
q: Built too strong For force or virtue ever to expugn.

senses.d: Active quality or power; capacity or power adequate to the production of a given effect; energy; strength; potency; efficacy; as, the virtue of a medicine.
q: Jesus, immediately knowing in himself that virtue had gone out of him, turned him about.
A man was driven to depend for his security against misunderstanding, upon the pure virtue of his syntax.
The virtue of his midnight agony.

senses.d: Energy or influence operating without contact of the material or sensible substance.
q: She moves the body which she doth possess, Yet no part toucheth, but by virtue's touch.

senses.d: Excellence; value; merit; meritoriousness; worth.
q: I made virtue of necessity.
In the Greek poets, . . . the economy of poems is better observed than in Terence, who thought the sole grace and virtue of their fable the sticking in of sentences.

senses.d: Specifically, moral excellence; integrity of character; purity of soul; performance of duty.
q: Virtue only makes our bliss below.
If there's Power above us, And that there is all nature cries aloud Through all her works, he must delight in virtue.

senses.d: A particular moral excellence; as, the virtue of temperance, of charity, etc.
Specifically: Chastity; purity; especially, the chastity of women; virginity.
q: H. I believe the girl has virtue. M. And if she has, I should be the last man in the world to attempt to corrupt it.

senses.d: One of the orders of the celestial hierarchy.
q: Thrones, dominations, princedoms, virtues, powers.

Virtue.etym: [OE. vertu, F. vertu, L. virtus strength, courage, excellence, virtue, fr. vir a man. See Virile, and cf. Virtu.]

senses.d: Possessing or exhibiting virtue.
Exhibiting manly courage and strength; valorous; valiant; brave.
q: Old Priam's son, amongst them all, was chiefly virtuous.

senses.d: Having power or efficacy; powerfully operative; efficacious; potent.
q: Lifting up his virtuous staff on high, He smote the sea, which calméd was with speed.
Every virtuous plant and healing herb.

senses.d: Having moral excellence; characterized by morality; upright; righteous; pure; as, a virtuous action.
q: The virtuous mind that ever walks attended By a strong siding champion, conscience.

senses.d: Chaste; pure; — applied especially to women.
q: Mistress Ford . . . the virtuous creature, that hath the jealous fool to her husband.

Virtuous.etym: [OE. vertuous, OF. vertuos, vertuous, F. vertueux, fr. L. Virtuous. See Virtue, and cf. Virtuoso.]

senses.d: The face, countenance, or look of a person or an animal; — chiefly applied to the human face.
q: His visage was so marred more than any man.
Love and beauty still that visage grace.

Visage.etym: [F. visage, from L. visus a seeing, a look, fr. videre, visum, to see. See Vision.]

senses.d: To face.
Perceivable by the eye; capable of being seen; perceptible; in view; as, a visible star; the least spot is visible on white paper.
q: Maker of heaven and earth, and of all things visible and invisible.
Virtue made visible in outward grace.

senses.d: Noticeable; apparent; open; conspicuous.
q: The factions at court were greater, or more visible, than before.

Visible.etym: [L. visibilis, fr. videre, visum, to see: cf. F. visible. See Vision.]

senses.d: The act of seeing external objects; actual sight.
q: Faith here is turned into vision there.

senses.d: The faculty of seeing; sight; one of the five senses, by which colors and the physical qualities of external objects are appreciated as a result of the stimulating action of light on the sensitive retina, an expansion of the optic nerve.
That which is seen; an object of sight.

Especially, that which is seen otherwise than by the ordinary sight, or the rational eye; a supernatural, prophetic, or imaginary sight; an apparition; a phantom; a specter; as, the visions of Isaiah.
q: The baseless fabric of this vision.
No dreams, but visions strange.

senses.d: Hence, something unreal or imaginary; a creation of fancy.

Vision.etym: [OE. visioun, F. vision, fr. L. visio, from videre, visum, to see: akin to Gr. � to see, � I know, and E. wit. See Wit, v., and cf. Advice, Clairvoyant, Envy, Evident, Provide, Revise, Survey, View, Visage, Visit.]

senses.d: To see in a vision; to dream.
q: For them no visioned terrors daunt, Their nights no fancied specters haunt.

senses.d: To go or come to see, as for the purpose of friendship, business, curiosity, etc.; to attend; to call upon; as, the physician visits his patient.
To go or come to see for inspection, examination, correction of abuses, etc.; to examine, to inspect; as, a bishop visits his diocese; a superintendent visits persons or works under his charge.
To come to for the purpose of chastising, rewarding, comforting; to come upon with reward or retribution; to appear before or judge; as, to visit in mercy; to visit one in wrath.
q: hath visited and redeemed his people.

Visit.etym: [F. visiter, L. visitare, fr. visere to go to see, to visit, fr. videre, visum to see. See Vision.]

senses.d: To make a visit or visits; to maintain visiting relations; to practice calling on others.

The act of visiting, or going to see a person or thing; a brief stay of business, friendship, ceremony, curiosity, or the like, usually longer than a call; as, a visit of civility or respect; a visit to Saratoga; the visit of a physician.
The act of going to view or inspect; an official or formal inspection; examination; visitation; as, the visit of a trustee or inspector.

Visit.etym: [Cf. F. visite. See Visit, v. t., and cf. Visite.]

senses.d: The act of visiting, or the state of being visited; access for inspection or examination.
q: Nothing but peace and gentle visitation.

senses.d: Specifically: The act of a superior or superintending officer who, in the discharge of his office, visits a corporation, college, etc., to examine into the manner in which it is conducted, and see that its laws and regulations are duly observed and executed; as, the visitation of a diocese by a bishop.
The object of a visit.

The act of a naval commander who visits, or enters on board, a vessel belonging to another nation, for the purpose of ascertaining her character and object, but without claiming or exercising a right of searching the vessel. It is, however, usually coupled with the right of search (see under Search), visitation being used for the purpose of search.
Special dispensation; communication of divine favor and goodness, or, more usually, of divine wrath and vengeance; retributive calamity; retribution; judgment.
q: What will ye do in the day of visitation?

senses.d: A festival in honor of the visit of the Virgin Mary to Elisabeth, mother of John the Baptist, celebrated on the second of July.
A light cape or short cloak of silk or lace worn by women in summer.
A call; a summons; a citation; especially, a designation or appointment to a particular state, business, or profession.
q: What can be urged for them who not having the vocation of poverty to scribble, out of mere wantonness make themselves ridiculous?

senses.d: Destined or appropriate employment; calling; occupation; trade; business; profession.
q: He would think his service greatly rewarded, if he might obtain by that means to live in the sight of his prince, and yet practice his own chosen vocation.

senses.d: A calling by the will of God.

The bestowment of God's distinguishing grace upon a person or nation, by which that person or nation is put in the way of salvation; as, the vocation of the Jews under the old dispensation, and of the Gentiles under the gospel.
A call to special religious work, as to the ministry.
q: Every member of the same , in his vocation and ministry.

Vocation.etym: [L. vocatio a bidding, invitation, fr. vocare to call, fr. vox, vocis, voice: cf. F. vocation. See Vocal.]

senses.d: Sound uttered by the mouth, especially that uttered by human beings in speech or song; sound thus uttered considered as possessing some special quality or character; as, the human voice; a pleasant voice; a low voice.
q: He with a manly voice saith his message.
Her voice was ever soft, Gentle, and low; an excellent thing in woman.
Thy voice is music.
Join thy voice unto the angel choir.

senses.d: Sound of the kind or quality heard in speech or song in the consonants b, v, d, etc., and in the vowels; sonant, or intonated, utterance; tone; — distinguished from mere breath sound as heard in f, s, sh, etc., and also whisper.
The tone or sound emitted by anything.
q: After the fire a still small voice.
Canst thou thunder with a voice like him?
The floods have lifted up their voice.
O Marcus, I am warm'd; my heart Leaps at the trumpet's voice.

senses.d: The faculty or power of utterance; as, to cultivate the voice.
Language; words; speech; expression; signification of feeling or opinion.
q: I desire to be present with you now, and to change my voice; for I stand in doubt of you.
My voice is in my sword.
Let us call on God in the voice of his church.

senses.d: Opinion or choice expressed; judgment; a vote.
q: Sic. How now, my masters! have you chose this man? 1 Cit. He has our voices, sir.
Some laws ordain, and some attend the choice Of holy senates, and elect by voice.

senses.d: Command; precept; — now chiefly used in scriptural language.
q: So shall ye perish; because ye would not be obedient unto the voice of the Lord your God.

senses.d: One who speaks; a speaker.
A particular mode of inflecting or conjugating verbs, or a particular form of a verb, by means of which is indicated the relation of the subject of the verb to the action which the verb expresses.

Voice.etym: [OE. vois, voys, OF. vois, voiz, F. voix, L. vox, vocis, akin to Gr. � a word, � a voice, Skr. vac to say, to speak, G. erwähnen to mention. Cf. Advocate, Advowson, Avouch, Convoke, Epic, Vocal, Vouch, Vowel.]

senses.d: To give utterance or expression to; to utter; to publish; to announce; to divulge; as, to voice the sentiments of the nation.
q: It was voiced that the king purposed to put to death Edward Plantagenet.

senses.d: To utter with sonant or vocal tone; to pronounce with a narrowed glottis and rapid vibrations of the vocal cords; to speak above a whisper.
To fit for producing the proper sounds; to regulate the tone of; as, to voice the pipes of an organ.
To vote; to elect; to appoint.
To clamor; to cry out.
Containing nothing; empty; vacant; not occupied; not filled.
q: The earth was without form, and void.
I 'll get me to a place more void.
I 'll chain him in my study, that, at void hours, I may run over the story of his country.

senses.d: Having no incumbent; unoccupied; — said of offices and the like.
q: Divers great offices that had been long void.

senses.d: Being without; destitute; free; wanting; devoid; as, void of learning, or of common use.
q: A conscience void of offense toward God.
He that is void of wisdom despiseth his neighbor.

senses.d: Not producing any effect; ineffectual; vain.
q: shall not return to me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please.
I will make void the counsel of Judah.

senses.d: Containing no immaterial quality; destitute of mind or soul.
Of no legal force or effect, incapable of confirmation or ratification; null. Cf. Voidable, 2.

Void.syn: Empty; vacant; devoid; wanting; unfurnished; unsupplied; unoccupied.
Void.etym: [OE. voide, OF. voit, voide, vuit, vuide, F. vide, fr. (assumed) LL. vocitus, fr. L. vocare, an old form of vacare to be empty, or a kindred word. Cf. Vacant, Avoid.]

senses.d: An empty space; a vacuum.
q: Pride, where wit fails, steps in to our defense, And fills up all the mighty void of sense.

senses.d: To remove the contents of; to make or leave vacant or empty; to quit; to leave; as, to void a table.
q: Void anon her place.
If they will fight with us, bid them come down, Or void the field.

senses.d: To throw or send out; to evacuate; to emit; to discharge; as, to void excrements.
q: A watchful application of mind in voiding prejudices.
With shovel, like a fury, voided out The earth and scattered bones.

senses.d: To render void; to make to be of no validity or effect; to vacate; to annul; to nullify.
q: After they had voided the obligation of the oath he had taken.
It was become a practice . . . to void the security that was at any time given for money so borrowed.

senses.d: To be emitted or evacuated.
A roll; a scroll; a written document rolled up for keeping or for use, after the manner of the ancients.
q: The papyrus, and afterward the parchment, was joined together to form one sheet, and then rolled upon a staff into a volume (volumen).

senses.d: Hence, a collection of printed sheets bound together, whether containing a single work, or a part of a work, or more than one work; a book; a tome; especially, that part of an extended work which is bound up together in one cover; as, a work in four volumes.
q: An odd volume of a set of books bears not the value of its proportion to the set.

senses.d: Anything of a rounded or swelling form resembling a roll; a turn; a convolution; a coil.
q: So glides some trodden serpent on the grass, And long behind wounded volume trails.
Undulating billows rolling their silver volumes.

senses.d: Dimensions; compass; space occupied, as measured by cubic units, that is, cubic inches, feet, yards, etc.; mass; bulk; as, the volume of an elephant's body; a volume of gas.
Amount, fullness, quantity, or caliber of voice or tone.

Volume.etym: [F., from L. volumen a roll of writing, a book, volume, from volvere, volutum, to roll. See Voluble.]

senses.d: In a voluntary manner; of one's own will; spontaneously.
Proceeding from the will; produced in or by an act of choice.
q: That sin or guilt pertains exclusively to voluntary action is the true principle of orthodoxy.

senses.d: Unconstrained by the interference of another; unimpelled by the influence of another; not prompted or persuaded by another; done of his or its own accord; spontaneous; acting of one's self, or of itself; free.
q: Our voluntary service he requires.
She fell to lust a voluntary prey.

senses.d: Done by design or intention; intentional; purposed; intended; not accidental; as, if a man kills another by lopping a tree, it is not voluntary manslaughter.

Of or pertaining to the will; subject to, or regulated by, the will; as, the voluntary motions of an animal, such as the movements of the leg or arm (in distinction from involuntary motions, such as the movements of the heart); the voluntary muscle fibers, which are the agents in voluntary motion.
Endowed with the power of willing; as, man is a voluntary agent.
q: God did not work as a necessary, but a voluntary, agent, intending beforehand, and decreeing with himself, that which did outwardly proceed from him.

senses.d: Free; without compulsion; according to the will, consent, or agreement, of a party; without consideration; gratuitous; without valuable consideration.
Of or pertaining to voluntaryism; as, a voluntary church, in distinction from an established or state church.

Voluntary.etym: [L. voluntarius, fr. voluntas will, choice, from the root of velle to will, p. pr. volens; akin to E. will: cf. F. volontaire, Of. also voluntaire. See Will, v. t., and cf. Benevolent, Volition, Volunteer.]

senses.d: One who engages in any affair of his own free will; a volunteer.
A piece played by a musician, often extemporarily, according to his fancy; specifically, an organ solo played before, during, or after divine service.
One who advocates voluntaryism.
To eject the contents of the stomach by the mouth; to puke; to spew.

Vomit.etym: [Cf. L. vomere, vomitum, and v. freq. vomitare. See Vomit, n.]

senses.d: To throw up; to eject from the stomach through the mouth; to disgorge; to puke; to spew out; — often followed by up or out.
q: The fish . . . vomited out Jonah upon the dry land.

senses.d: Hence, to eject from any hollow place; to belch forth; to emit; to throw forth; as, volcanoes vomit flame, stones, etc.
q: Like the sons of Vulcan, vomit smoke.

senses.d: Matter that is vomited; esp., matter ejected from the stomach through the mouth.
q: Like vomit from his yawning entrails poured.

senses.d: That which excites vomiting; an emetic.
q: He gives your Hollander a vomit.

Vomit.etym: [L. vomitus, from vomere, vomitum, to vomit; akin to Gr. �, Skr. vam, Lith. vemiti. Cf. Emetic, Vomito.]

senses.d: A solemn promise made to God, or to some deity; an act by which one consecrates or devotes himself, absolutely or conditionally, wholly or in part, for a longer or shorter time, to some act, service, or condition; a devotion of one's possessions; as, a baptismal vow; a vow of poverty.
q: I pray thee, let me go and pay my vow.
I am combined by a sacred vow.

senses.d: Specifically, a promise of fidelity; a pledge of love or affection; as, the marriage vow.
q: Knights of love, who never broke their vow; Firm to their plighted faith.

Vow.etym: [OE. vou, OF. vou, veu, vo, vu, F. v�u, from L. votum, from vovere, to vow. Cf. Avow, Devout, Vote.]

senses.d: To give, consecrate, or dedicate to God, or to some deity, by a solemn promise; to devote; to promise solemnly.
q: that vow a long and weary pilgrimage.

senses.d: To assert solemnly; to asseverate.

Vow.etym: [OE. vouen, OF. vouer, voer, F. vouer, LL. votare. See Vow, n.]

senses.d: To make a vow, or solemn promise.
q: Better is it that thou shouldest not vow, than that thou shouldest vow and not pay.

senses.d: Formerly, a passage either by sea or land; a journey, in general; but not chiefly limited to a passing by sea or water from one place, port, or country, to another; especially, a passing or journey by water to a distant place or country.
q: I love a sea voyage and a blustering tempest.
So steers the prudent crane Her annual voyage, borne on winds.
All the voyage of their life Is bound in shallows and in miseries.

senses.d: The act or practice of traveling.
q: Nations have interknowledge of one another by voyage into foreign parts, or strangers that come to them.

senses.d: Course; way.

Voyage.etym: [OE. veage, viage, OF. veage, viage, veiage, voiage, F. voyage, LL. viaticum, fr. L. viaticum traveling money, provision for a journey, from viaticus belonging to a road or journey, fr. via way, akin to E. way. See Way, n., and cf. Convey, Deviate, Devious, Envoy, Trivial, Viaduct, Viaticum.]

senses.d: To take a voyage; especially, to sail or pass by water.
q: A mind forever Voyaging through strange seas of thought alone.

senses.d: To travel; to pass over; to traverse.
q: With what pain voyaged the unreal, vast, unbounded deep.

senses.d: Any one of numerous species of rapacious birds belonging to Vultur, Cathartes, Catharista, and various other genera of the family Vulturidæ.

Vulture.etym: [OE. vultur, L. vultur: cf. OF. voltour, F. vautour.]
